questions.question: A database, replicas, and backups stay in the approved country, but the provider's foreign identity root can reset customer administrators. What has the design proved?
options: Full operational sovereignty
Data residency, but not independent identity authority
Provider exit readiness
That lawful-access risk is eliminated
questions.explanation: Local copies can satisfy a residency boundary while the foreign identity root still controls a critical administrative decision.

questions.question: What should happen before an architect converts a law or contract into cloud controls?
options: Select the provider with the most local regions
Assume every data category has the same rule
Copy a certification statement into the architecture
Have accountable legal and risk owners define a workload-specific control contract
questions.explanation: Architecture enforces a defined contract; it should not invent legal scope or treat a provider label as legal analysis.

questions.question: Which design gives the customer meaningful identity authority during a provider account outage?
options: A customer-rooted identity service with independent revocation and tested emergency access
A second administrator in the same provider identity tenant
A local data center with no administrator audit trail
A longer password for the provider root account
questions.explanation: An independent root and revocation path keep identity decisions usable when the normal provider account plane is unavailable.

questions.question: Why is customer-managed encryption insufficient when the provider can release or bypass keys unilaterally?
options: The ciphertext is stored too close to the application
Key rotation always moves data abroad
The customer does not hold an effective deny capability over plaintext access
Encryption prevents backups from being restored
questions.explanation: Key sovereignty depends on who can authorize use or deny access, not only whose name appears on the key resource.

questions.question: A placement policy checks the primary database location but ignores indexes, logs, and support bundles. What is the main failure?
options: The policy has too many evidence records
It leaves ungoverned data surfaces that may cross the residency boundary
It prevents provider support from authenticating
It makes the workload portable
questions.explanation: Derived and operational copies can contain regulated data, so every data surface belongs in the placement contract.

questions.question: Which evidence best proves why a sensitive workload was admitted to a platform?
options: The immutable policy version, workload identity, evaluated controls, decision, and resulting resource locations
A screenshot of the provider region selector
The current service marketing page
A list of all employees
questions.explanation: Decision evidence must connect the workload and policy version to evaluated controls and observed placement.

questions.question: Which break-glass design remains credible when provider identity and control-plane services are unavailable?
options: An undocumented shared root password
A provider support ticket that requests root access
A backup stored behind the same failed provider identity
Separate local credentials, dual approval, isolated backups, a clean recovery environment, and immutable logging
questions.explanation: The emergency path must avoid the failed dependencies while retaining authorization, containment, evidence, and post-use accountability.

questions.question: Which result most strongly demonstrates exit portability?
options: A contract says exports are available
A backup file was created inside the source provider
A timed rehearsal restored portable data, schemas, identity mappings, keys, and infrastructure on an alternate target
The source platform has three availability zones
questions.explanation: A successful timed restore on a different target proves that the exported data and operational dependencies can actually be reconstructed.
